Sales & Promotions

Written exactly as you type it. Keep it short — it has to read across a booth on the kiosk.

Why bother

Right now this is a page in your browser, and browser tabs get lost. On your home screen it becomes an icon like any other app: one tap, no address to remember, no searching through tabs on a market morning. It opens full screen and stays signed in.

Nothing is installed and nothing is downloaded from a store. It is the same page, with a door of its own.

iPhone and iPad

Use Safari. This does not work from Chrome or Firefox on an iPhone — if you are reading this in another browser, copy the address into Safari first.

1. Tap the Share button
The square with an arrow coming out of the top. At the bottom of the screen, or top right on an iPad.
2. Scroll down the list and tap Add to Home Screen
It sits below the row of apps, among Add Bookmark and Find on Page.
3. Tap Add, top right
You can shorten the name first if you like — “IFM” fits better under the icon.

The icon lands on your home screen. Open it from there from now on.

Android

Use Chrome, or whichever browser you normally use — most Android browsers can do this, and the wording varies a little between them.

1. Tap the three dots, top right
Some phones show a small “Install” banner instead. If you see one, tap that and you are done.
2. Tap Add to Home screen
It may read Install app or Install. Same thing.
3. Tap Add or Install to confirm
Some phones then offer to place it for you, or let you drag it where you want it.

The icon lands on your home screen. Open it from there from now on.

If it looks stuck on an old version

The app updates itself when the market puts up a new version, and tells you when it does. If it ever seems to be behind, close it completely and open it again — on an iPhone, swipe up from the bottom and flick the app away first. That is the only maintenance it needs.

The Next Two Months

The Schedule

A customer hands you a gift certificate. Take what they are spending; the rest stays on their certificate for another day.

How This Settles

What you take goes straight onto your account with the market as money the market owes you, the same as any payment the office records for you. The certificate was paid for at the office window when it was sold, so you are not waiting on the customer for anything. You do not need to bring the certificate to the office — the customer keeps it until it is empty.

The app records what you enter here. Nothing checks it against the customer, so enter what they actually spent.

Fictional charges and credits for every vendor, so the Monthly Statements tool can be looked at with something in it. These live in their own record and are never written into the real fines, day fees or gift certificates — switching them off leaves nothing behind, and every line shows a demo mark wherever it appears.

Before Handing the App to the Market

Press Wipe. The Beta Reset tool clears these too, but Wipe is the one that says what it does. Once wiped, the statement tool shows only what the market actually recorded.

Points decide the order vendors are called in for a booth, so a point added or taken away changes who gets which stall. The office enters them — it knows who worked a PopUp — and they wait here. Until you sign one off it counts for nothing.

Waiting on You

Something the market could do better, or something worth trying. It does not have to be finished, and it does not have to be a proposal — the office and the Board President read these, and anything worth taking further can become one later.

Ideas Sent

The Merch Mansion’s stock book and till. Ring items up through the market day, then close out once — the day goes to the market’s records in a single go, so a busy stand never slows the app down for everyone else.

One statement a month for every vendor: what they were charged, what they paid or were credited, and where they stand on points and hours. Built from the market’s records each time it is opened, so a correction anywhere corrects the statement too.

Whose Statement

Exception Requests for the Board

The Guide’s Special Needs Requests. The Board decides these; the office passes them on and records the answer. An approved one is what removes the up-to-$100-a-market charge for an attendance shortfall, so a decision nobody wrote down is a charge nobody can explain later.

Lines a Vendor Says Are Wrong

Every statement ends by inviting this. Correcting does not erase — the original line stays and a dated correction sits beside it with the reason, so a statement already sent still makes sense.

For the end of the month, when every vendor gets one. To deal with a single vendor, find them above.

Look Up a Certificate

Not for ordinary redemptions. A certificate is not meant to come back here: the customer keeps it until it is empty, and a vendor takes what they are owed at their own stall with their own phone. This is for the cases that need the office:

  • a vendor who cannot scan — no phone, flat battery, no signal — who brings it to the window
  • a customer paying a daily stall fee with it
  • somebody asking what is left on one
  • voiding one, if you have its serial
  • cashing out the last few dollars, which New York requires under $5 on request

Scan it, or type the code printed on it.

The serial is the only way in. A certificate records its number, amount and date — not who bought it — so if somebody has lost one and cannot tell you the serial, there is nothing here to look it up by. Ask whether they photographed it or kept the receipt. Whether the market replaces a lost certificate at all is a question for the Board, not something this screen decides.

Sell a Certificate

Set the amount, then scan the certificate. Keep scanning to sell more at the same amount.

dollars

Tap a usual amount or type any other. A certificate is loaded with whatever the customer asks for — there is no ceiling in the app, and nothing in the Guide sets one.

Load a Roll of Certificate Codes

Before a batch can be sold from, its codes go in here. A code the app has never seen cannot be sold or redeemed, which is what makes a forged one useless.

Two ways to get the codes in. If the printer sent a list, paste it. If they did not — and many do not — scan the stickers in with the camera, one after another; the camera stays open so you can work through a sheet.

Whatever you want to call it. Nothing is printed on the stickers — this is just so the office can tell one batch from another later.

The printed Guide is a yearly snapshot; the board amends continuously. After each meeting, record anything rule-bearing here in one line — and record the quiet months too, so silence means “confirmed no change,” not “unknown.” This log is also next year’s Guide revision, built as it happens.

The booths deliberately held back from the season-long reservations, so that there is always something to give a vendor who does not hold a booth. They go out first in the Thursday round and stay in the pool for the in-person rounds after it. The Guide calls these the “unreservable” booths, which names what cannot be done with them rather than what they are for.

    Design questions that were settled in conversation, recorded so they stay settled. When a change is proposed that touches one of these, the principle is the starting position — it can be overturned, but only knowingly.
    

    

    

    

    

    

    After a Major Change, Sweep These
    

    A rename, a moved tool, or a rephrasing ripples further than the screen it happens on. This is the sweep list — each entry is a place stale wording has actually been found.
    

    Debugging means running the Self-Audit, not remembering a list
    A fault found by hand once will be found by hand every time unless it is written into runSelfAudit. Ten faults live there now, and three were added the day they were first found by hand: a help dot over an empty entry (promises an answer, gives a blank) or a written entry no screen can open (seven of over seven hundred characters each were sitting unreachable); a drawer that opens onto nothing, because its tool draws only after somebody types (this hid Points Manager); and the desk order naming a drawer that is gone, nested or renamed, where the key is ignored in silence. Two traps when adding a check: measure textContent, never innerText — an inactive screen is display:none and innerText reads empty for every one of them, which made the first version call the whole app blank; and await a turn of the event loop after runScreenInit, since screens that fill themselves from storage are not done when it returns. A check that cries wolf gets ignored, so prove a new one both catches the real fault and stays quiet on a clean app.
    

    Never print a title the header already printed
    The header names whoever is at the desk; a screen title saying the same words directly beneath it is repetition, and it has been shipped twice (“Market Manager” over “Market Manager”, then “Board President” over “Board President”). The rule is enforced in renderScreenHead: any title matching the header’s name is suppressed, on every screen, automatically. Do not work round it with a hand-written <h1> in the markup — the rule cannot see those.
    

    A screen is described in five places
    Change what a tool is and five separate texts go stale, each written at a different time and none of them next to the others in the file. Walk all five, every time:

    • The desk tile — the folder entry in MGR_FOLDERS, or the drawer’s fold-sub on the vendor desk.

    • The screen’s own intro — the empty-note under its heading.

    • The help dot — its entry in HELP_TEXTS, found by index and easy to mismatch. Read the title as well as the body: entry 45 sat under the wrong screen’s name for months.

    • Plain Words — if the market has its own name for the thing.

    • Anywhere else that names it — alerts, Records Needed, planned-tool explainers, other tools’ summaries.

    Absence Patterns was rebuilt to watch deadlines rather than count absences, and for two builds the tile, the help dot and Plain Words all still described the leaderboard it had stopped being. A screen that contradicts its own description teaches people not to trust either.
    

    Help dots
    Every “?” whose screen changed. A rebuilt screen can orphan its help dot entirely — check the dot still exists, and that its text describes the screen as it now stands.
    

    Explainers behind cones
    Planned-tool text that names other tools, desks, or old vocabulary — including the footer state when a cone comes off.
    

    Plain Words
    If the market’s vocabulary moved, the ledger records it — old word kept in quotation marks as the bridge.
    

    App Glossary
    If the app’s own vocabulary moved — a desk renamed, a new kind of part invented — the glossary follows.
    

    Every debt and credit reaches a statement
    There are eleven ways money can land on a vendor’s account: fines entered by hand, fines the ladder derives, booth-check fines, booth fees for each of the four venues, the statement’s own late fee, the membership share, work hours not worked, and the late renewal surcharge on the debit side; SNAP tokens turned in, gift certificates taken at a stall, booth fees paid at the window, checks, cash, card at the desk and Square on the credit side. A new one must be added to accountData or it silently never bills. An audit of this list found four holes at once: Wednesday and Winter fees charged nothing because the season calendar only makes Saturdays and Sundays, SNAP had no route at all, and the January renewal surcharge was filed as due the following December.
    

    One stray </div> can wreck half the app silently
    Every screen must sit inside <main>, which carries the page’s side padding. A single extra closing tag ends <main> early and every screen defined after it renders flush to the edge of the phone — while everything before it looks perfect, so the app appears fine on the desk you happen to be testing. Build 16-86 did exactly this when a wrapper was removed by scanning for its matching tag, and it broke the whole manager and president desk while the vendor desk was untouched. Never delete a wrapper by counting tags in a script; and run t27-structure.js, which checks div balance across the file and that no screen has escaped <main>.
    

    Nothing may run off the side of the phone
    Cards, rows and text carry max-width:100% and overflow-wrap:anywhere; a flex text column carries a floor (min-width: min(100%, 14rem)) so a sibling input cannot squeeze it to one letter a line. Use overflow-wrap: break-word, never anywhere, on anything holding a title: anywhere lets the browser count a single character as an element’s minimum width, so a flex row squeezed “My Account” into “My Accou / nt”. anywhere is reserved for the few places a single unbroken string can genuinely exceed the phone — a certificate code, a run-together vendor name in a report row. Test with t24-overflow.js, which walks every screen in every role at 390px and 320px and reports anything past the edge, and with t25-titles.js, which checks no drawer title is narrower than its own longest word. It found 98 at first pass. The kiosk booth map is excluded on purpose: it is wider than the phone by design and is dragged, not read.
    

    Removing the last item leaves the box
    Take the only entries out of a card and the card remains, rendering as a blank white box on the screen. Nothing throws and no other test notices. t29-emptycards.js walks every screen in every role and reports any card with no text and no control in it. A card filled by a renderer that only runs for some roles should start hidden and be revealed by that renderer, rather than sitting empty for everyone else.
    

    A superseded tool leaves its door behind
    When a new tool replaces an old one, the old way in usually survives — a tile in a folder, a drawer on a desk, a button in a card. Each is correct on its own and nothing throws, so only a person noticing catches it. t28-duplicates.js is that person: it walks every desk in every role and reports two doors onto one screen, one name opening two tools, and screens nothing opens. A second door that is deliberate goes in its ALLOWED list with the reason, so intentional repetition is declared rather than argued about again later. Run it after removing or replacing any tool.
    

    One way to choose a vendor
    Any <select> holding the vendor list is fitted automatically with a search box and a list of tappable matches; the dropdown itself is hidden but stays in the page holding the value, so anything reading sel.value or listening for change keeps working. A tool needs to do nothing to get this. Options that are not vendors — “choose”, “Nobody” — are kept and offered as their own rows, since those are real choices. Never build a second search box beside a vendor list by hand.
    

    A screen opens at the top of itself
    Changing screen resets the scroll, and so does entering a desk — otherwise a desk reached from halfway down a long tool opens halfway down. Drawers are deliberately exempt: toggleToolFold anchors the scroll to the drawer being opened so it does not jump under the finger. If a new container ever scrolls instead of the window, add it to scrollAppToTop.
    

    One way back
    Every control that goes back a step wears the pointing hand: the crumb, the role picker, and any button inside a screen. Build one with makeBackButton(label, onclick), or mark it class="back-link" data-backhand="1" and the hand is drawn on screen open. Test with t26-backhand.js. Three controls deliberately do NOT wear it, because the hand means go back and they are actions: Close the selection ends a Booth Selection, Put everything back to the Guide resets the rules, and ‹ Prev steps a calendar to the previous month. A left chevron paired with Next is a stepper, not a way back. A back button without the hand makes "back" look like two different things depending where the person is standing.
    

    Crumbs and desk homes
    A moved tool must crumb back to its new desk, and nothing should still say where it used to live.
    

    Cross-references in other tools’ text
    Summaries, alerts, tile descriptions and Records Needed entries that name the changed thing by its old name.
    

    Screens shared between desks
    A screen reachable from more than one desk carries every control it has to whoever opens it. Season-Long Booth Reservations sits on the vendor desk as well as the manager’s, and shipped Assign & Advance, Pass, and Release to vendors. Any control that writes the market’s records — rather than the person’s own — needs the manager-only class and a requireManager() check inside the function, because hiding a button does not withhold the power behind it. The vendor desk has now been swept; staff, volunteer and kiosk have not. See BF15. Two questions to ask of any card on a shared screen: does this person need it, and is it theirs to see? A card can pass the second and fail the first — that is how a manager’s ledger of booth holdings ended up on a vendor’s desk.
    

    Retiring a tool
    Before removing one, prove the thing that replaced it actually reaches the same place. Add a Vendor to This Saturday was retired once it was shown end to end that a booth request entered in Manual Input puts the vendor in Saturday’s pool by the same route as one sent from a phone — and that is the better route, because it carries how the request arrived and when the vendor told the office. Sunday keeps its own version: that desk is a sign-in sheet at the 8:30 meeting and nothing else feeds it, so removing it there would take away the only way in. Sweep the tool’s id out of the screen registry too, and guard whatever used to reach for it. One thing must not be deleted: a HELP_TEXTS entry, because every help dot is numbered by position and removing one silently moves all the rest — mark the slot retired and leave it.
    

    A screen that needs a record the app may not hold yet
    Draw first, fetch second. A screen that opens with await loadSomething() before it writes anything to the page will show nothing at all while that one fetch is outstanding — not a spinner, not a heading, nothing — and a person tapping it will say the tool is frozen. It is not frozen; it is being polite to a fetch that most of the screen does not depend on. This bites hardest on a new storage key, because until somebody writes to it the sheet has no row and every phone fetches it separately and gets a cold Apps Script. Draw everything already in hand, then call the loader and redraw when it lands. A write still waits, because writing into a half-known list would drop whatever had not arrived. Others that still open this way, should they ever feel slow: initUnreservableScreen, initFeePayScreen, renderTaskManager, renderAvailableTasks, renderOrgStalls.
    

    A new tool on the Market Manager’s desk
    Two desks are built two different ways, and a tool added to one does not appear on the other. The staff desk is hand-written drawers in the markup. The Market Manager desk is generated from the tool registry — the list of groups and tiles — so a manager tool has to be added there, whatever the markup says. SNAP Tokens In & Out was written into the markup alone and turned up on the staff desk only, where nobody was looking for it. When testing, look inside the drawer the tool is meant to be in: a document-wide search for the title finds it on the wrong desk and reports success.
    

    Anything that floats over the app
    A sheet, a backdrop, a pop-up: give it modal-backdrop, let freeFloatingSheets() move it to the body at boot, and show it by adding the class open — never by copying another sheet’s markup and hoping. .modal-backdrop is display:none until opened, which it was not always: it used to be display:flex, so a new backdrop was on screen from boot unless whoever added it also wrote a rule to hide it. That shipped once, and because a backdrop covers everything at z-index:500 it did not look like a stuck sheet, it looked like the whole app had stopped working. Defaults should fail closed. Written inside the screen that first needed it, it works from that screen and nowhere else — and it fails in silence, because display:flex on a box whose ancestor is display:none throws nothing and logs nothing. It presents as an unrelated part of the app being broken: this was reported as “the map is not clickable booth by booth”, and the map was never the problem. The seventh fault names any that escape.
    

    A new live map, or a new layer on an old one
    Add it to AUDIT_MAPS. The map knows a great deal — the buildings, the promenade panels, the section labels, the badge on every booth, the placed furniture and outlets — and a screen that leaves half of it out still looks like a map, which is why the sixth fault counts layers instead of trusting the eye. Where a map is meant to carry less, say so in its without list along with the reason, so a real gap cannot hide behind “that one is different”.
    

    A booth on any map
    Every booth on every live map opens the booth sheet, and every booth means every booth — including ones already spoken for. A booth that is taken is exactly the booth a vendor rings up to ask about, and a chip that does nothing is the office being told to go and look it up somewhere else. The sheet takes a context saying which desk it was opened from, and offers that desk’s action inside it; where there is no action, it still says everything known about the booth. A map that offers less than another map is a fault, not a simplification.
    

    A card that takes an entry and reports back
    Mark it desk-form. When the desk changes hands — one vendor to another, vendor to manager, anyone to the kiosk — clearDeskState() empties every field inside it, along with every .status-msg on the page. Without the mark, nothing sweeps it, and the next person opens the tool to find the last person’s words and the last person’s green confirmation. A block whose text is worked out from state rather than typed — a running total, a note that appears only for certain days — gets desk-transient instead. Clearing empties such a block; it must never hide it. An earlier version set display:none on sweep and nothing ever unset it, so after a hand-over the next render wrote into an invisible box: the office scanned a certificate, was told what was on it, and saw none of the buttons for doing anything with it. An empty block takes no space on its own. A field that must survive a hand-over because it shows a saved setting rather than something part-typed gets keep-on-handover. The Self-Audit’s fifth fault names any card it finds unenrolled, so this is checkable rather than remembered.
    

    Correcting a seeded record
    Changing a value in BOOTH_SEED, DEMO_VENDORS_SEED, REQUIREMENT_SEED or the Winter dates now reaches sheets that already exist — but only where nobody has edited that field. Adding a new collection to the seed means adding it to SEED_MERGE as well, or its records become permanent the first time they are written. And when a seed value changes for a record that may already be in the wild under the old value, name the old value in LEGACY_SEED_BIRTH so sheets written before the stamps existed can still be corrected. Watch the size of the birth keys: booths and vendors sit near 22,000 characters against a cell limit around 50,000.
    

    Reconcilers correct, they do not invent
    Code that repairs records on load may clear a value that cannot be true, but must never fill in a different one. reconcileBoothReservations used to turn an ineligible Saturday reservation into a Sunday-only booth, granting a vendor a holding they never won at any auction, silently, on every load. Clearing is honest; substituting is a fabrication that later reads as fact.
    

    Map piece kinds
    Placed pieces record only the kind’s key, and the pieces themselves live in the sheet, not in the build. Renaming or removing a kind orphans every piece already placed under the old key — so a kind’s key is permanent even when its label changes.
    

    Beta Reset must not ship
    Any build headed for real market use sets BETA_RESET_TOOLS to false. The reset desk rewrites records for every phone; it exists only to clean up after testing. A new storage key must also be added to BETA_RESET_KEYS as traffic or as configuration — a key in neither group is silently spared, and the screen’s three lists are drawn from that same table.
    

    The handoff document
    The next session inherits whatever the handoff says — it must describe the app as shipped, not as remembered.

    How Long Things Wait
    

    These decide how the app feels rather than what it does. Every one was a guess when it was written, and every one is better settled by standing in front of the thing at the market than by reasoning about it. Changes take effect at once — no reload — so you can watch the difference.
    

    

    

    



    


    

    

    Two That Matter Beyond Feel
    

    How often the app asks the sheet
    This one is not taste. At 168 phones, every second you take off it multiplies: shorter means fresher records and more load on a Google Apps Script that answers one caller at a time, and a market morning is when both matter most. The shipped 11 seconds carries a random extra of up to a fifth on each phone, deliberately — without that scatter they would all ask in the same second. This is the number to settle before a real rollout.
    

    Shortest the loader will show
    Not a delay. It is a floor that stops the sunflower appearing and vanishing before your eye has settled on it, which reads as a fault. Set it to nothing and quick fetches will flicker.
    

    

    

    

    

    

    Pretend It Is Another Day
    

    Much of this app only does anything on a particular date — the Sunday sign-in window, the Wednesday absence deadline, posting a sale, the season rolling over. This makes the whole app believe it is a day of your choosing so you can see those things without waiting for them.
    

    





    Leave the time blank and the real clock keeps ticking on the pretend day. Name a time to sit at a particular moment — 8:29 AM on a Sunday, say.
    

    

    



    

    

    

    What This Does Not Protect You From
    

    Worth reading once.
    

    Anything you save is saved for real
    Record an absence while pretending it is next Sunday and a real record is written to the market’s sheet, dated next Sunday, visible to the office and to that vendor. That is deliberate — a testing mode that quietly threw writes away would prove nothing about whether saving works — but it means you have to clean up after yourself.
    

    It is this device only
    Nobody else’s phone is affected, and it does not travel through the sheet. Your friend testing on Android will still be in the real week.
    

    It stays on until you turn it off
    Closing the app does not clear it. The purple band across the top is there so this is never a surprise.
    

    

    

    

    

    

    How This Opening Went
    

    A cold open used to wait for the whole sheet before showing anything. It now opens from a copy kept on this device and corrects itself when the sheet answers. When it is slow, this says which part was slow — guessing at that from somewhere else is how two weeks get wasted.

    Nearly every leak found in testing has belonged to one of seven faults, and each one can be looked for by machine. Reports were being fixed one instance at a time while the rest of the class sat undisturbed — this walks the whole population instead. It cannot judge whether wording is good, only whether it is consistent, and it knows nothing of faults nobody has named yet.

    How This Works
    

    The app fills an empty sheet with invented records so the market can be seen working before the real ones arrive. Every seeded field is stamped with the value it was born with. On each load, a field still matching its stamp is still the app’s own invention, so a build that corrects it delivers the correction. A field that no longer matches was changed by somebody — it keeps their value and loses its stamp, permanently. Fields the seed never set are never touched at all.

    Handover
    

    The app is being built on a personal Google account. When the
Ithaca Farmers Market takes it over they start a fresh backend on an account they control. This is the list
of what must change hands, and what must be created new rather than transferred.
    

    The rule that decides each item: anything that can spend the market’s money,
read its payment records, or lock its members out belongs to an account the market controls

    Serving the App From the Phone
    

    Written, tested, and switched off. index.html is about 2.2 MB, 644 KB over the wire, and GitHub Pages sets no long cache header on it — so today every visit downloads and parses the whole thing before anything appears, and iOS drops backgrounded tabs, which makes “every visit” most of them.
    

    Measured with it on: 692 ms cold against 367 ms warm, and the app opens with no network at all — which matters at Steamboat Landing, where the signal is poor and the market is busiest exactly when it is worst. It also ends the mid-deploy 404: GitHub Pages serves real 404s for about two minutes after an upload, and with this a vendor gets the previous build, working, instead of nothing.
    

    What it costs is a second file. A service worker cannot be registered from inside the page that registers it, so sw.js has to sit beside index.html. That makes a deploy two uploads instead of one, and uploading index.html without sw.js would leave the old worker serving the old app. That is the whole reason it is off.
    

    To switch it on: save the code below as sw.js next to index.html, replace __BUILD_ID__ with the build number, and set SERVICE_WORKER_ON = true in this file. Do both, or neither. From then on every deploy is two files and the build number must change in both.
    

    It never reloads the app under somebody: a new build is fetched quietly and a bar offers it. This app takes money, and swapping the code mid-correction is worse than a stale page.
    

    // Ithaca Farmers Market Vendor Portal -- service worker
//
// Build: __BUILD_ID__   (stamped by build.py; do not edit by hand)
//
// WHAT THIS IS FOR. index.html is about 2.2 MB, 644 KB over the wire. Without
// this, every visit downloads and parses the whole thing before the app can
// draw anything, and the person watches a spinner. GitHub Pages sets no long
// cache header on index.html, and iOS Safari evicts backgrounded tabs, so
// "every visit" means most of them.
//
// With this, the app is served from the device. The spinner appears once
// after a deploy instead of every time, and the app opens with no signal at
// all -- which matters at Steamboat Landing, where the phone signal is poor
// and the market is busiest exactly when the network is worst.
//
// IT ALSO FIXES THE MID-DEPLOY 404. GitHub Pages serves genuine 404s for
// about two minutes after an upload. Today that means a vendor who opens the
// app in that window gets nothing. Here, a failed fetch falls back to the
// cached copy: they get the previous build, working, instead of an error.
//
// WHAT IT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT DO. It never swaps the running code under
// somebody. This app takes money and records attendance; a page that reloads
// itself while a manager is halfway through a correction is worse than a
// stale page. A new build is fetched quietly, and the person is told there is
// one and taps when they are ready.

const BUILD = '__BUILD_ID__';
const CACHE = 'ifm-' + BUILD;

// Only what the app needs to start. Everything else it uses is inside
// index.html already, which is the point of a single-file app.
const SHELL = ['./', './index.html'];

self.addEventListener('install', event => {
  event.waitUntil((async () => {
    const cache = await caches.open(CACHE);
    // One at a time and forgiving: a precache that rejects as a whole means
    // no service worker at all, and a partly warm cache beats none.
    await Promise.all(SHELL.map(async url => {
      try { await cache.add(new Request(url, { cache: 'reload' })); } catch (e) {}
    }));
    // Deliberately NOT skipWaiting. A new worker waits until the person asks
    // for it, so the code under a half-finished task never changes.
  })());
});

self.addEventListener('activate', event => {
  event.waitUntil((async () => {
    const keys = await caches.keys();
    await Promise.all(keys.map(k => (k !== CACHE && k.indexOf('ifm-') === 0)
      ? caches.delete(k) : Promise.resolve()));
    await self.clients.claim();
  })());
});

// The page asks for the new worker when the person taps the banner. Until
// then this one keeps serving, whatever is waiting.
self.addEventListener('message', event => {
  if (event.data === 'ifm-activate-now') self.skipWaiting();
});

self.addEventListener('fetch', event => {
  const req = event.request;
  if (req.method !== 'GET') return;

  const url = new URL(req.url);
  if (url.origin !== self.location.origin) return;

  // The backend is the Google Apps Script and must never be cached: it holds
  // the sheet, and a cached answer is a wrong balance.
  if (url.pathname.indexOf('/macros/') !== -1) return;

  // Anything that navigates -- opening the app, a bookmark, a scanned QR --
  // is answered from the cache first and refreshed behind the person's back.
  const isPage = req.mode === 'navigate' ||
    (req.headers.get('accept') || '').indexOf('text/html') !== -1;

  event.respondWith((async () => {
    const cache = await caches.open(CACHE);
    const hit = await cache.match(isPage ? './index.html' : req, { ignoreSearch: isPage });

    // Refresh in the background either way. The person is not waiting on it,
    // so a slow network costs them nothing.
    const fresh = fetch(req).then(res => {
      if (res && res.ok && res.type === 'basic') {
        cache.put(isPage ? './index.html' : req, res.clone()).catch(() => {});
      }
      return res;
    }).catch(() => null);

    if (hit) return hit;

    const res = await fresh;
    if (res) return res;

    // No cache, no network. For a page this is the only honest answer, and
    // it says what to do rather than showing the browser's dinosaur.
    if (isPage) {
      return new Response(
        '<!doctype html><meta charset="utf-8">' +
        '<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1">' +
        '<style>body{font:16px/1.5 -apple-system,system-ui,sans-serif;' +
        'background:#EFEDE3;color:#23231B;margin:0;padding:48px 24px;text-align:center}' +
        'b{display:block;font-size:19px;margin-bottom:8px}</style>' +
        '<b>No signal, and nothing saved yet</b>' +
        'The app has not been opened on this phone before, so there is no copy ' +
        'on it to fall back to. Try again where there is a signal &mdash; once it ' +
        'has loaded here once, it will open without one.',
        { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'text/html; charset=utf-8' }, status: 503 });
    }
    return Response.error();
  })());
});

    


    

    

    Sending Statements Without Pasting
    

    A mail link cannot send anything. It asks the office’s own mail program to open a draft, in plain text, with no attachment and no formatting — which is why the statement has to be pasted in. Nothing on the browser side changes that.
    

    The way round it is for the backend to send: the market’s Apps Script already holds the sheet, already runs as the market’s own account, and can send mail. Add the code below and the Send it buttons appear on the statements screen. Until then they stay hidden and the drafting route is offered instead.
    

    Two things to know before switching it on. First, this is the app sending on the market’s behalf rather than opening a draft for a person to read — so it keeps a preview and a confirm, and records what went and when, but the office is no longer reading each one before it goes. Second, Google caps sending: 100 messages a day on an ordinary Gmail account, 1,500 on a Workspace one. With 168 vendors, a market on ordinary Gmail sends a month across two days. The app asks the script what is left and stops before it is refused halfway.
    

    Whose address it comes from is whoever owns the script. That is the same rule as everything else on this screen: it should be an account the market controls, not a personal login.
    

    // Add to the market's Apps Script, then Deploy > Manage deployments > New
// version. Nothing else in the app changes; the Send buttons light up on
// their own once this answers.
//
// Put this INSIDE the existing doGet / doPost, alongside the sheet handling.

function ifmMailCheck() {
  return { ok: true,
           from: Session.getEffectiveUser().getEmail(),
           remaining: MailApp.getRemainingDailyQuota() };
}

function ifmSendMail(p) {
  if (!p || !p.to || !p.html) return { ok: false, error: 'missing to or html' };
  if (MailApp.getRemainingDailyQuota() < 1) {
    return { ok: false, error: 'the daily sending quota is used up' };
  }
  MailApp.sendEmail({
    to: p.to,
    subject: p.subject || 'Ithaca Farmers Market statement',
    htmlBody: p.html,
    body: p.text || '',
    name: 'Ithaca Farmers Market'
  });
  return { ok: true };
}

// In doGet, before the sheet lookup:
//   if (e.parameter.action === 'mailcheck') {
//     return ContentService.createTextOutput(JSON.stringify(ifmMailCheck()))
//       .setMimeType(ContentService.MimeType.JSON);
//   }
//
// In doPost, after JSON.parse(e.postData.contents) into `body`:
//   if (body.action === 'sendmail') {
//     return ContentService.createTextOutput(JSON.stringify(ifmSendMail(body)))
//       .setMimeType(ContentService.MimeType.JSON);
//   }
    


    

    

    Who Owns This
    

    The market can own this app outright, and should record that it does. Under Anthropic’s terms the outputs Claude produced belong to the person who commissioned them — Anthropic claims no ownership, there is no license tying this code to Claude, and nothing in the app contacts Anthropic or needs Claude to run. It is a plain file on the market’s hosting talking to the market’s spreadsheet. As between the builder and the market, ownership is a one-line board minute; this card is here so a future board knows there is nothing else to clear.
    

    In practice, owning software like this means controlling the accounts. That is the rule at the top of this screen: the repository under a market-owned organization, the backend on a market-controlled Google account. Whoever holds those holds the app, whatever any document says.
    

    No maintainer is built in. The app was written so the market is not tied to Claude, to Anthropic, or to any one developer: one file, no build step, no framework, no dependencies, ordinary JavaScript, with the reasoning behind decisions recorded inside the app itself — the Principles desk, the PLANNED registry, the board flags, this checklist, and comments in the code that explain why rather than what. A year with no new features needs no developer at all: fees, fines, deadlines, the work-hour rate, venues and rosters are all changed from inside the app by the office and the Board. New features and bug fixes need a developer — Claude is the convenient one because it already knows the project, but any competent web developer can maintain a single self-documenting file. The honest caveat for a human maintainer: it is one very large file, and the settling-in takes longer than the usual project — the records named above are what shorten it.
    

    One murky edge, stated rather than hidden: code generated by AI has uncertain copyright standing in the United States. The market’s real protection is not a certificate but possession — it holds every line, in the most portable format there is, on accounts it controls.
    

    

    

    

    

    

    Records Needed
    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    Improving Your Booth
    

    

    Drawings and specifications go to the Buildings & Grounds Committee before construction, in person or by email, at least one week before their meeting.     Report Harassment or Discrimination
    

    Under the market’s Sexual Harassment Policy this goes straight to the Market Manager or a Board officer — president, vice president, secretary or treasurer — who must open a prompt investigation and keep it confidential so far as they can. Retaliation against anyone who reports is prohibited and is itself grounds for discipline.
    

    If there was unwanted physical touching, confinement, or coerced sexual contact, that may be a crime. You can call the local police, and you can do that instead of or as well as this. You may also file with a government agency or in court — using either of these does not give any of that up.
    

    Neither of these is stored in the app, on purpose — a report of this kind should not sit in a list, and once sent you could not take it back.
    
 The market’s complaint form
 Email the Market Manager directly

    That opens your own email app. You do not have to use this at all — telling the Market Manager or any board officer in person carries exactly the same weight.

    Exceptions & Accommodations
    

    

    Exception Request — the Guide calls this the “Special Needs Request”
    

    Asks the Board to allow something the rules otherwise do not: a late fee, a shortfall against the attendance requirement, a Leave of Absence, a disability accommodation. It is a policy exception, whatever the reason.
    

    



    



    


    The Board decides these, not the office. The office passes it on; nobody at the window can grant one, and the Guide says plainly that they are not automatically granted.
    

    

    

    

    

    

    Business & Ownership
    

    

    Report an Ownership Change
    

    The Guide requires you to tell the Market Manager about a planned change — a sale, a partner joining or leaving, or a change in how profit and loss is shared — in a timely manner.
    

    







    


    The Board decides what this means for the business, not the office. A change of five percent or less, or a death, bankruptcy, divorce, or a transfer among spouses, children or grandchildren, is usually exempt from further review; anything more goes to committee and the Board, who may decide the business must re-enter as a new vendor of equal status.

    Value-Added Farm Products Application — the Guide calls these “Enhanced Agricultural Products”
    

    For Ag vendors adding a made product (jam, cider, baked goods, etc.) built from what they grow. At least 75% of the finished product must be a farm-grown ingredient. Goes to the Ag Committee for jurying.

    Some of the market’s oldest words describe something other than what actually happens. Where a word misleads, the app uses a plainer one and keeps the Guide’s word beside it.     Every value here is the rule as written, whether or not
anyone has been enforcing it lately. When practice and paper disagree, this is the paper — the thing
a manager or the Board can point to when a decision needs justifying. Each row names the document it
comes from.
    

    

    

    What Changed
    



    

    Nothing has been changed from the Guide.
    


    

    

    

    What This Screen Cannot Change
    

    This screen changes numbers and dates. It cannot change how the market works.
    

    Adding a booth request to Sunday, reordering who chooses first in a Booth Selection, adding a new approval step, changing who a rule applies to, or adding a screen — all of that is a change to the app itself and needs whoever maintains it. The same goes for anything not listed above: if a number is not on this screen, it is still written into the code.
    

    Two things this screen does not do on its own. It does not rewrite a season that has already closed — a fee changed today does not restate last year’s invoices. And on a device with no shared storage, a change made here stays on that device.
    

    New licenses, permits and certificates do not belong here at all: add those in Vendor Requirements, which was built for exactly that.

    Bylaws VI §2: the President appoints committee chairpersons, and may name the members or leave that to the chair. This screen records those appointments so the rest of the app knows who to route work to — it does not make them. The office keeps the record; the President makes the decision.
    

    

    Committee
    

    Changing anything here is the Board President's, not the Market Manager's. Bylaws Article VI §2 gives the President the appointment; you can read who serves and what is in front of each committee, but adding, removing, naming a chair, and forming a new committee are the President's to do.

    What This Screen Can and Cannot Do
    

    Committee membership is subject to Board approval, and chairs are
appointed by the Board President (Bylaws, Article VI). This screen records those
decisions so everyone can see them — it does not make them. Add people here
after the Board has said yes, not before.
    

    Time served on a committee counts toward a vendor’s work hour
requirement. Hours are logged through Log Hours You Worked on the vendor’s own desk and
signed off by the Market Manager — the committee chair keeps the meeting tally and passes it on,
as the Food Committee guidelines describe. Tasks a chair posts to the board are the exception:
those confirmations go to the chair.
    

    Chairs post jobs directly now. With the rosters recorded here, the app can
tell a chair from any other vendor, so each chair has a posting card on their own Committees drawer.
A task they post goes to the whole board in the committee’s name, and when a vendor reports it
done the confirmation comes back to the chair who posted it — the person who can actually see
whether the work is done — rather than to the office. The manager’s board still shows every
task and names where each confirmation goes.

    Out by 4 PM today
    

    

    The pavilion is rented after market today. Every vendor must have their booth
space packed, cleaned and clear by 4 PM — not just the selling stopped, but out.
    

    

    This is the Vendor Guide’s rule for rental days (p.17).
Plan your pack-up so the space is clear on time.
